newsitem.title: UK: World financial watchdog not viable - BOE adviser.
newsitem.headline: World financial watchdog not viable - BOE adviser.

text.p: Regulating financial markets may be a world-wide problem, but a global watchdog is not the answer, according to a report to central bankers released on Monday.
"Nobody is suggesting or contemplating a global regulator," Charles Goodhart told a conference outlining a paper presented to a central bank governors' meeting at the Bank of England last week.
Goodhart, a professor at the London School of Economics (LSE), was last week appointed as a member of the Bank of England's new monetary policy committee.

He pointed out the huge financial costs on countries around the world of banking crises, drawing on IMF figures which showed 133 member countries had experienced significant banking sector problems between 1980 and 1986.
And more global markets demand new approaches.

"Increasing globalisation of banking and finance means that autarky is no longer a viable approach in financial regulation: regulation determined at the national level can be undermined by developments in other regulatory jurisdictions," the report said.
While this was leading to increasing degrees of harmonisation, there was a danger this could make regulation uniformly bad rather than creating efficient and viable collaboration, it added.

The debate over international regulation was given added urgency by the collapse of British merchant bank Barings in February 1995 after Singapore-based trader Nick Leeson ran up losses totalling around $1.4 billion in unauthorised derivatives trades.
Financial scandals since then have added to this drive for greater international co-operation to prevent a break-down of the increasingly inter-linked financial markets.

Goodhart and his co-authors concluded the focus should be the objectives of regulation -- systemic stability and consumer protection -- and the extent to which they can be secured more efficiently through international collaboration.
But there was a danger of harmonisation being pursued for its own sake, taking it beyond the point where benefits exceed costs.
"There are many reasons why, in some areas, differences in regulation between countries are both viable and desirable," the paper said.

These include allowing for different social choices to be made, for different institutional structures and potential for systemic hazard and for differences in certain regimes and how these would impact on other systems, and the social cost of institutional failure.

"Competition in regulation can be beneficial providing systemic stability is not impaired and the externalities of one regime do not impose costs on others," central bank governors were told last week.
The report suggests general guidelines for dealing with the international dimension of financial regulation, but stresses these should not form a straight-jacket.

It proposes agreed minimum standards for the safety and soundness of relevant institutions, particularly in the areas of minimum capital adequacy standards and requirements for analysing risk and management systems.

Clear and agreed mechanisms for sharing relevant information between regulators about the financial standing and business operations of firms under their jurisdiction are also essential, the report said.
International co-operation is needed in investigating problem firms and where it is necessary to close an institution this should not be impeded by international barriers.

Firms need to have an agency which is clearly responsible for overall regulation, monitoring and supervision and there should be no scope for them to dodge minimum standards by moving to areas where regulation is lax.

A lead regulator must be identified for all financial conglomerates with international business "so that all other regulators know, without any uncertainty, who is the relevant regulatory agency", the report said.
